title: Convergent validity and AVE
summary: The average variance extracted measures how much of its indicators' variance a reflective construct explains on average; .50 or more is the usual heuristic.

body.text: [[convergent-validity]] asks whether the indicators of a reflective construct converge on one thing. Its usual measure is the average variance extracted, [[ave]] (Fornell & Larcker 1981).

body.explanation: The mean of the squared standardised loadings of the k indicators: the average share of indicator variance explained by the construct.

body.text: An AVE of .50 or more means the construct explains at least half of its indicators' variance on average (Fornell & Larcker 1981; Hair et al. 2022). Like loadings, classic PLS AVE values are inflated for reflective constructs: in the TAM example PEOU has AVE .662 under PLS and .551 under PLSc. AVE is not defined for formative constructs.

mistake.title: Treating .49 and .51 as different verdicts
mistake.text: The .50 threshold is a convention. Report the value, consider its uncertainty and the estimator (PLS inflates AVE), and do not delete items only to step over the line.

tryIt.task: Run the TAM example with PLS-SEM and with PLSc. Compare the AVE of each construct under both estimators.

checks.question: Three indicators load .90, .70 and .50. What is the AVE?

options.feedback: .70 is the mean loading. AVE averages the squared loadings.
That is the square of the mean loading (.70²). Square first, then average.

checks.question: Should you report AVE for a composite-formative index?

options.text: No. AVE assumes a common factor behind the indicators, which an index does not posit.
options.feedback: Correct. SEM Lab shows AVE as not applicable for such blocks.
Index components need not share variance, so a low AVE carries no message about quality.
Reporting a criterion only when it looks good is selective reporting; here the criterion does not apply at all.
